adds.title: LGBTQ rights in the Philippines - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Wikipedia's LGBTQ rights in the Philippines page is the national-framework document a visitor stands under in Eastern Visayas (national law applies uniformly across the region's six provinces) and it records the only Eastern-Visayas-specific datapoints located: in Northern Samar, two of the province's 24 municipalities were reported (circa 2012) to be run by openly LGBTQ mayors, and Leyte is among the provinces listed as having LGBTQ elected officials. The page also fixes the national legal baseline for the region: there is no general anti-discrimination law at national level while numerous LGU-level SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances exist elsewhere in the country, transgender people may not change their legal gender, same-sex marriage is not recognized (the Family Code defines marriage as between 'a man and a woman'), and the SOGIE Equality Bill has remained pending in Congress since the 2000s. This confirms the record's assessment that Eastern Visayas shows local LGBTQ political participation but no legal deviation from the national position.

adds.title: LGBTQ rights in the Philippines - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Wikipedia's LGBTQ rights in the Philippines page frames what a visitor to Northern Mindanao stands under: no general national anti-discrimination law (only piecemeal local ordinances), transgender people may not change their legal gender, same-sex marriage is not recognized (the Family Code confines marriage to 'a man and a woman'), and the SOGIE Equality Bill remains pending in Congress. Citing MindaNews (24 June 2019), the page notes that only 4 local government units across all of Mindanao had passed pro-LGBT ordinances by mid-2019, consistent with the record's caution that the absence of a Northern Mindanao regional signal reflects sparse documentation rather than confirmed absence of divergence (including in Lanao del Norte, where the record notes adjacent Muslim personal-law courts operate).
